title: Coordinated inheritance of extrachromosomal DNAs in cancer cells
source: Science TLDR podcast episode 12 show notes
one_line: Shows that distinct extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) species in cancer cells are inherited together during mitosis rather than randomly, driven by intermolecular interactions and transcription.
key_claims: Distinct ecDNA species co-segregate non-randomly into daughter cells at mitosis, producing correlated inheritance rather than independent assortment.
Co-segregation is mediated by physical intermolecular interactions between ecDNA species, notably within ecDNA hubs.
Active transcription at the onset of mitosis facilitates ecDNA co-segregation.
Coordinated inheritance supports oncogene co-amplification and co-selection, including specialised 'enhancer-only' ecDNAs that carry regulatory elements but no oncogene and act in trans.
Coordinated inheritance shapes responses to targeted therapy, with ecDNA integration into chromosomes noted as a route to escape drug pressure and co-inheritance.
limitations: Show notes report no specific quantitative measurements of co-segregation frequency or effect sizes.
Precise molecular mechanism linking transcription to co-segregation (specific protein factors) is not identified.
Whether coordinated inheritance extends to other extrachromosomal elements such as viral episomes or biomolecular condensates was not tested.
Interactions beyond pairs of ecDNA species (higher-order co-assortment) were not resolved.
Long-term consequences of ecDNA co-inheritance under continuous versus intermittent drug exposure were not established.
open_questions: Identify the transcription-associated factors that tether ecDNA species together at mitosis and test whether their loss randomises segregation.
Test whether simultaneously targeting co-segregating oncogene pairs prevents resistance better than single-agent therapy.
Determine whether chromosomal integration of ecDNA is a reproducible escape route under sustained drug pressure.
Quantify the contribution of coordinated inheritance to intratumoural heterogeneity and cancer evolution in vivo.
